10.1002_advs.77065: Artificial synapses capable of analog memory and adaptive learning are key components for neuromorphic computing systems. To emulate biological synaptic functions effectively, artificial devices must exhibit gradual conductance modulation, linear responses to pulse stimuli, diverse forms of synaptic plasticity, and low-power operation. Ion-mediated electrochemical devices have recently emerged as promising candidates for such functionalities because ionic redistribution can continuously modify the internal electrochemical state of materials and naturally produce history-dependent conductance changes. This review discusses recent advances in battery-ion-inspired synaptic devices that exploit electrochemical processes to implement artificial synaptic behavior. We first outline the fundamental electrochemical mechanisms underlying ion-mediated state modulation, including ion insertion/accumulation, intercalation, migration, and diffusion. We then survey the materials landscape for battery-inspired synaptic devices, covering electrolytes and active channel materials such as transition metal oxides, two-dimensional materials, and organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors. Emerging applications in neuromorphic computing and neuromorphic biosensing are revisited, where ionic dynamics enable the integration of sensing, memory, and computation. Key challenges related to device reliability, scalability, and environmental stability are discussed, together with future perspectives for advancing battery-ion-based neuromorphic technologies.
10.1016_j.marpolbul.2026.119344: Understanding the environmental fate and behaviour of microplastics across space and time is challenging, especially in remote locations such as the Galápagos Islands. Citizen science can support plastic monitoring by extending geographic and temporal coverage, though concerns persist around data validation. This study evaluated a simple citizen science methodology, aided by a near-infrared portable spectrometer (PlasTell), for the rapid monitoring of beach microplastics (>1 mm) to investigate spatiotemporal accumulation patterns on Tortuga Bay, Santa Cruz Island, Galápagos. A total of 3377 suspected microplastics were collected by citizen scientists between 2020 and 2025. ATR-FTIR spectroscopy verified that 92.77% of particles had been correctly identified as plastic, primarily low-density polyethylene (72.51%) and polypropylene (22.44%) fragments. The mean microplastic concentration on Tortuga Bay was 145.29 ± 23.57 particles m −2 , which increased significantly in 2024 (290.88 ± 73.76 particles m −2 ), coinciding with the El Niño-Southern Oscillation in the Pacific Ocean. Accumulation gradients both parallel and perpendicular to the waterline were observed, with four-fold higher concentrations and elevated pre-production pellet (‘nurdle’) composition at the turtle nesting zone at the back of the beach (234.59 ± 42.25 particles m −2 , 22.54% respectively). Despite more limited characterisation potential, PlasTell identified 89.24% of microplastics in <1 s with no false positives, overcoming the analytical bottleneck of microplastics for researchers and enabling timely data validation. Subsequently, this study demonstrates how technology aided citizen science methodologies can fill major regional knowledge gaps on microplastic accumulation, compensating for climatic complexity and environmental variability, to support plastics monitoring efforts in remote island systems.
10.1021_acsami.6c07527: Electrochromic tungsten oxide (WO3) films are promising candidates for flexible smart window applications. However, realizing large-area WO3-based electrochromic devices fabricated by low-temperature solution processing remains challenging. Here, we report a roll-to-roll (R2R)-compatible strategy for the fast fabrication of electrochromic WO3 films by synergistically combining an ultrafast intense pulsed light (IPL) process with trace Pt additives acting as light absorbers. Pt-incorporated WO3 (WO3-Pt) films were coated onto flexible substrates and subsequently treated within 10 ms using intense broadband irradiation from a xenon flash lamp. Structural, optical and chemical analyses indicate that the IPL process promotes the photothermal modification of WO3, while the Pt additive significantly enhances photothermal heating efficiency and electronic conductivity of the WO3 films. When integrated into electrochromic devices, the IPL-treated WO3-Pt (WO3-Pt-IPL) films exhibit high optical contrast, accelerated switching kinetics, and enhanced cycling stability compared to bare and IPL-treated WO3 films without Pt. The electrochromic device based on WO3-Pt-IPL film exhibited the highest optical contrast of 61.5% at 550 nm and a coloration efficiency (CE) of 139 cm2 C-1, whereas the devices based on bare WO3, WO3-Pt, and WO3-IPL films showed lower optical contrast values of 55.5%, 59.7%, and 59.3%, respectively, with CE values of around 80 cm2 C-1. In addition, the WO3-Pt-IPL device maintained nearly constant bleached and colored transmittance over 1500 cycles, demonstrating markedly improved cycling stability compared with the other device configurations. We further demonstrate large-area fabrication of WO3 films via R2R slot-die coating combined with IPL processing, achieving excellent spatial uniformity. This approach enables energy-efficient and scalable production of flexible metal oxide films and provides a feasible pathway for tuning charge transport and electrochromic properties in electrochromic materials.
10.1021_acscatal.6c03505: Commercialization of electrochemical nitrogen reduction (eNRR) is hindered by limited catalyst performance, the lack of scalable electrochemical cell architectures, and an incomplete understanding of performance-limiting processes. This work aims to address these challenges through a systematic investigation of catalyst composition and microstructure, device configuration, and reaction mechanisms. Molybdenum (Mo) metal single atoms and clusters supported on mesoporous nitrogen-doped carbon were synthesized with tunable pore sizes via a five-second photothermal pyrolysis of a self-assembled bottlebrush block copolymer (BBCP) template. For eNRR, improved Mo dispersion enhanced electrochemical accessibility, while the coexistence of atomically dispersed Mo species and Mo clusters produced a structurally heterogeneous catalytic environment that benefits eNRR. A gas-diffusion electrode (GDE) flow cell was constructed for continuous operation testing; the catalyst–device system achieved a Faradaic efficiency of 21.6% and an ammonia yield rate of 34.7 μg h–1 mg–1. Intermediate pore sizes and balanced electrode wettability promoted effective triple-phase boundary formation and active-site utilization. Electrochemical characterization combined with machine-learning analysis of flow-cell parameters indicated that activation polarization is the dominant loss mechanism, governed primarily by intrinsic active-site kinetics and electrochemically accessible surface area. In contrast, pore size, metal dispersion, and electrode wettability primarily regulate site accessibility rather than mass-transport limitations. Together, these results provide a framework linking catalyst structure, electrode architecture, and kinetic limitations in eNRR flow-cell systems and offer practical design guidelines for advancing scalable eNRR technology.
